newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Stora paints gloomy forest picture.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Stora paints gloomy forest picture.

text.p: Swedish forestry company Stora said on Wednesday lower prices and reduced deliveries sent its 1996 profits plummeting, giving a sneak preview of a cheerless reporting season for forestry stocks.
Stora posted a 1996 profit of 2.35 billion crowns ($320.8 million) compared to 8.02 billion crowns a year earlier. Turnover totalled 45.16 billion crowns versus 57.11 billion in 1995.
With the result coming in below market expectations of a profit of 2.55 billion crowns after net financial items, the share fell two crowns to close at 93.5.
"The report was somewhat lower than expectations but there was no news really," said Erik Magnusson, an analyst at Nordbanken.
"People are now waiting to hear what SCA will say, but they will just tell the same story," Magnusson said.

Rival forestry company SCA AB, or Svenska Cellulosa Aktiebolaget, is due to publish its 1996 result on January 30. MoDo will report its 1996 result on February 19, followed by AssiDoman AB the next day.
Stora said lower prices and lower delivery volumes negatively affected 1996 profits by 4.7 billion crowns and the stronger crown was behind a 750 million crown decrease.
Managing Director Lars-Ake Helgesson said volumes would rise in the next two years but gave no forecast.
"The volumes will climb in 1997, but especially in 1998," he told a news conference.
But several analysts were sceptical about his optimism.
"The volumes will be up this year because they can't be as bad as they were last year," Magnusson said.
"1997 seems to be a lost year, just like 1996," said Enskilda Securities forestry analyst Lars Kjellberg.
Kjellberg said the 1996 result was weighed down with investment costs which would spill over into the first half of this year but agreed there was room for improvement in 1998.
"In the first half of 1997 they are again going to be burdened with these extraordinary items," Kjellberg said.
"There is some scope for improvement in 1998 if European GDP growth does not go down again," Kjellberg said.
Analysts are divided on the burning question about when pulp prices will rise.
"They are going to collapse in the next three months," predicted Mads Asprem, forestry analyst at Morgan Stanley.
Magnusson of Nordbanken said the markets were waiting for North American Scandinavian pulp inventories to fall.
"It has to come down by 500,000 to 600,000 tonnes before we can see any increases in pulp for example," Magnusson said.
"But that will take at least a quarter from now. I don't foresee any price increases for pulp in the first half of 1997. June-July maybe," Magnusson said.
Swedbank forestry analyst Mikael Jafs said there could be pressure on pulp prices short-term but that price increases could take place in the spring.
"Historically, what we've seen in March, April and May is that producer inventories come down," Jafs said.
($1=7.325 Swedish Crown)
